title: Replicating BEIR
summary_easy: Tanay rebuilt the main experiment of BEIR, a benchmark showing that neural search models trained on one dataset often lose to plain keyword search on new kinds of documents. On two scientific datasets every published number he checked came back, and a newer 2023 model beat keyword search on both. The one number that first missed led him to a library default that silently cut every document to 100 tokens; fixing it matched the paper exactly.
summary_deep: An independent reproduction of Thakur et al. 2021 on SciFact (5,183 documents, 300 queries, binary, 1.1 relevant per query) and NFCorpus (3,633 documents, 323 queries, graded, 38.2 relevant per query) using the official BEIR release. BM25 is a Python reimplementation with Anserini's k1 = 0.9 and b = 0.4, Lucene idf, Porter stemming and the 33 word Lucene stopword list; TAS-B and DPR run through sentence-transformers with dot product, bge-small-en-v1.5 with cosine and its query instruction, and reciprocal rank fusion (k = 60) combines BM25 and TAS-B. Metrics come from pytrec_eval. The four dense cells land within 0.001 nDCG@10 of the paper (three exactly) and BM25 is off by +0.012 and -0.005, attributed to single field indexing and exact lengths. DPR on SciFact first scored 0.260 against 0.318; a TAS-B control cleared the pipeline, an encoding ablation showed title only equalled title plus text, and a length sweep showed the context encoder port's max_seq_length of 100 was truncating abstracts. At 512 word pieces, BEIR's own setting, it matched 0.318 nDCG@10 and 0.727 Recall@100. bge-small beats BM25 on both datasets, and the hybrid beats both inputs. The headline run takes 12 minutes on a MacBook.

sheet.easy:
## What it is
An independent rebuild of BEIR's central experiment: do neural search models trained on one dataset lose to plain keyword search (BM25) on new kinds of documents? Two scientific datasets, run on one MacBook.

## Data
| | SciFact | NFCorpus |
|---|---|---|
| documents | 5,183 abstracts | 3,633 medical papers |
| test queries | 300 scientific claims | 323 short health questions |
| relevant per query | 1.1 (yes or no) | 38.2 (graded) |

## Systems
- BM25: keyword scoring, Python rewrite with the paper's settings.
- TAS-B and DPR: the paper's neural models.
- bge-small (2023, not in the paper) and a BM25 + TAS-B fusion (not in the paper).

## Results (nDCG@10, published / reproduced)
| | SciFact | NFCorpus |
|---|---|---|
| BM25 | 0.665 / 0.677 | 0.325 / 0.320 |
| TAS-B | 0.643 / 0.643 | 0.319 / 0.319 |
| DPR | 0.318 / 0.318 | 0.189 / 0.188 |
| bge-small | 0.713 | 0.343 |
| hybrid RRF | 0.687 | 0.341 |

## The bug
DPR on SciFact first scored 0.260. Its document model was set to read only 100 tokens, so most of every abstract was ignored, with no warning. Title only scored the same as title plus abstract, which gave it away. At 512 tokens it scored 0.318, exactly the paper. On NFCorpus the headline score hid the bug.

## How to say it
- Six of six published cells reproduced; three exact, a fourth within 0.001, BM25 off by +0.012 and -0.005.
- The paper holds for its models; a 2023 model beats BM25 on both datasets.
- Check document length against the model limit in any RAG system.

## Next
Significance tests, BM25 + bge fusion, Java BM25, capped recall, more datasets.
sheet.deep:
## Claim under test
BEIR (Thakur et al. 2021): dense retrievers trained on MS MARCO lose to BM25 zero shot. Published nDCG@10 for these datasets: SciFact BM25 0.665, DPR 0.318, ANCE 0.507, TAS-B 0.643, ColBERT 0.671, BM25+CE 0.688; NFCorpus 0.325, 0.189, 0.237, 0.319, 0.305, 0.350 (`published.json`).

## Data (official BEIR zips, `src/beirdata.py`)
| | SciFact | NFCorpus |
|---|---|---|
| corpus | 5,183 | 3,633 |
| test queries | 300 | 323 |
| relevance | binary | 3 level graded |
| relevant per query | 1.1 | 38.2 |
| avg query / doc words | 12.37 / 213.63 | 3.30 / 232.26 |
Only judged test queries are scored.

## BM25 (`src/bm25.py`)
$$\mathrm{score}(q,d)=\sum_{t\in q}\ln\!\Big(1+\frac{N-df_t+0.5}{df_t+0.5}\Big)\frac{tf_{t,d}(k_1+1)}{tf_{t,d}+k_1(1-b+b\,|d|/\mathrm{avgdl})},\quad k_1=0.9,\ b=0.4$$
Tokens `[a-z0-9]+`, lowercase, 33 Lucene stopwords, Porter (PyStemmer), numpy postings, argpartition top 100, zero scores dropped. Deviations from Anserini: one concatenated field (Anserini: title and body separately), exact lengths (Lucene: one byte norms), regex tokeniser. Lucene's own defaults are $k_1=1.2$, $b=0.75$.

## Dense (`src/dense.py`)
| model | encoder(s) | pooling | similarity | doc text | limit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| TAS-B | msmarco-distilbert-base-tas-b (6 layer) | CLS | dot | title + " " + text | 512 |
| DPR Multi | separate question and ctx BERT base | CLS | dot | title + " [SEP] " + text | 512 (port ships 100) |
| bge-small-en-v1.5 | one encoder, 33.4M, 384 dim | CLS | cosine (normalised) | title + " " + text; query instruction | 512 |
Exact search: query blocks of 64, `block @ doc_matrix.T`, argpartition top 100. Cost $O(QNd)$; encoding dominates.

## Metrics (`src/evaluate.py`, pytrec_eval)
$$\mathrm{nDCG@10}=\frac{1}{|Q|}\sum_q\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{10} g_i/\log_2(i+1)}{\mathrm{IDCG@10}}\quad\text{(linear gain = qrels grade)}$$
$$R@100=\frac{1}{|Q|}\sum_q\frac{|\mathrm{top}_{100}\cap\mathrm{Rel}_q|}{|\mathrm{Rel}_q|},\qquad R_{cap}@100:\ \text{denominator}\ \min(100,|\mathrm{Rel}_q|)$$
Plain equals capped on every SciFact query; capped is at least plain on NFCorpus.

## RRF (`rrf`, Cormack et al. 2009)
$$\mathrm{RRF}(d)=\sum_{r}\frac{1}{60+r(d)}$$
Inputs: BM25 and TAS-B top 100; ties broken by doc id; output top 100. Rank based, so no score normalisation.

## Results (`runs/final/report.json`)
| system | SciFact nDCG@10 pub / mine | SciFact R@100 pub / mine | NFCorpus nDCG@10 pub / mine | NFCorpus R@100 pub / mine |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| BM25 | 0.665 / 0.677 (+0.012) | 0.908 / 0.929 | 0.325 / 0.320 (-0.005) | 0.25 / 0.246 |
| TAS-B | 0.643 / 0.643 | 0.891 / 0.891 | 0.319 / 0.319 | 0.28 / 0.280 |
| DPR (512) | 0.318 / 0.318 | 0.727 / 0.727 | 0.189 / 0.188 | 0.208 / 0.208 |
| bge-small | n/a / 0.713 | n/a / 0.942 | n/a / 0.343 | n/a / 0.311 |
| RRF BM25+TAS-B | n/a / 0.687 | n/a / 0.948 | n/a / 0.341 | n/a / 0.294 |
Exactness: three of six nDCG@10 cells exact at three decimals, DPR NFCorpus within 0.001, BM25 +0.012 / -0.005; four dense Recall@100 cells exact.

## The truncation bug
First full run: DPR SciFact 0.260 (R@100 0.584) against 0.318 (0.727). Control: TAS-B exact. Ablation at the shipped `max_seq_length = 100`: space 0.260, [SEP] 0.276, text only 0.171, title only 0.261 (the tell). Sweep with [SEP]:
| limit | nDCG@10 | R@100 |
|---|---|---|
| 100 | 0.276 | 0.601 |
| 256 | 0.298 | 0.687 |
| 350 | 0.315 | 0.710 |
| 512 | 0.318 | 0.727 |
Space join at 512: 0.310. Length worth +0.042 to +0.050; [SEP] worth +0.008 to +0.016. BEIR uses the first 512 word pieces for all neural models; DPR was trained on 100 word passages with title [SEP]. NFCorpus: nDCG@10 0.191 buggy vs 0.188 fixed (hidden), R@100 0.190 vs 0.208 (visible); encoding 45.7 s vs 181.3 s.

## Verification
Official data and counts; judged queries only; pytrec_eval; `published.json` with table sources; per cell deltas with a 5e-4 zero threshold; TAS-B as positive control; DPR fix matched on two metrics.

## Runtime (MacBook, MPS)
Final run 19:48:02 to 19:59:55 UTC (about 12 minutes). SciFact / NFCorpus seconds: BM25 0.5 / 0.3, TAS-B 94.2 / 87.9, DPR 219.5 / 181.3, bge 70.4 / 58.6. DPR sweep about 20 minutes.

## Limitations
2 of 18 datasets; Python BM25; plain recall; no significance tests; single configurations for bge and RRF; bge contamination cannot be excluded.

narration.script:
BEIR's claim is that dense retrievers trained on MS MARCO look great in domain but lose to BM25 when you move them to a new domain with no training data. I rebuilt that on the two smallest scientific datasets, SciFact and NFCorpus, using the official data, and the document and query counts match the paper.

I ran five systems. BM25 is my own Python version with Anserini's settings, k1 0.9 and b 0.4, Porter stemming and Lucene's stopwords. TAS-B and DPR are the paper's dense models, scored with dot product because that's how they were trained. Then two additions, labelled as such: bge-small from 2023, and reciprocal rank fusion of BM25 and TAS-B. Metrics come from pytrec_eval, the same trec_eval bindings the paper used.

Results: the paper holds for its models. BM25 beats TAS-B and DPR on both datasets. TAS-B came back exactly, 0.643 and 0.319. BM25 was off by plus 0.012 and minus 0.005, which I attribute to indexing one field instead of two. bge-small beats BM25 on both datasets, so the gap has since closed. The hybrid beat both of its inputs.

The interesting part was DPR on SciFact: 0.260 against 0.318. TAS-B matching through the same code told me the pipeline was fine. I tried four document encodings, and title only scored the same as title plus abstract. That means the abstract wasn't being read. The DPR context encoder port ships with a 100 token limit. At 512, which is what BEIR used, DPR matched 0.318 and its recall matched too.

On NFCorpus the bug was invisible in nDCG, because each query has about 38 relevant documents. Next I'd add significance tests and a BM25 plus bge hybrid.

narration.prompt: Give me the full technical story, as you would to a staff engineer.
narration.script:
The target was the core result of BEIR, Thakur et al. 2021: dense retrievers trained on MS MARCO generalise badly zero shot, and BM25 stays a strong baseline. The paper evaluates on 18 datasets. I took the two smallest scientific ones so everything fits a laptop: SciFact, 5,183 abstracts and 300 claims with about one relevant abstract each, and NFCorpus, 3,633 medical documents and 323 short health questions with about 38 graded relevant documents each. I load the official BEIR zips and score only judged test queries, which is what BEIR does, and the counts match the paper.

BM25 is my own Python implementation, because Anserini needs Java and the machine didn't have it. It matches the paper's parameters, k1 0.9 and b 0.4, Lucene's idf, Porter stemming and Lucene's 33 word stopword list. It differs in two ways I document: one concatenated field instead of separate title and body fields, and exact document lengths where Lucene quantises them to one byte. The dense side uses sentence-transformers with a per checkpoint spec. TAS-B and DPR use dot product and CLS pooling because that's how they were trained. bge-small uses cosine and its query instruction. Search is exact: a matrix product in blocks of 64 queries, then the top 100. Metrics come from pytrec_eval, so the metric implementation is the same as the paper's, and published values live in a JSON file with their table source so every cell prints a delta.

Five of six paper cells came back on the first full run. TAS-B was exact on both datasets. BM25 was off by plus 0.012 and minus 0.005, opposite signs, which looks like implementation noise from the field and length differences. DPR on NFCorpus was fine. DPR on SciFact was 0.260 against 0.318, with recall 0.584 against 0.727.

The debugging went in order. TAS-B exact through the same loader, metrics and search code was a positive control, so the fault had to be DPR specific. I listed the candidates: the title and text join, the asymmetric encoders, and how much of each document the context encoder sees. Then I ablated four encodings at the shipped settings. Title only scored 0.261 and title plus text 0.260. If adding the abstract changes nothing, the abstract isn't being read. The ablation script logs max_seq_length at load: the DPR context encoder port ships with 100 tokens, while SciFact abstracts average over 200 words. Sweeping 100, 256, 350 and 512 with DPR's own title [SEP] format climbed to 0.318 and recall 0.727 at 512, matching both metrics to three decimals. BEIR's setup section says it feeds every neural model the first 512 word pieces, so that's the paper's real condition. Most of the gap was length; the separator token added about 0.008 to 0.016.

Why NFCorpus hid it: with about 38 relevant documents per query, the top 10 stays full of relevant hits even when the ranking is damaged, so nDCG@10 read 0.191 against 0.189. Recall@100 did show it, 0.190 against 0.208, which I'd now treat as an early warning.

Beyond the paper, bge-small beats BM25 on both datasets, 0.713 and 0.343, so the gap the paper found has closed, with a contamination caveat I state. RRF over BM25 and TAS-B beat both inputs and gave the best SciFact recall, 0.948. The whole table runs in 12 minutes on a MacBook. Gaps I'd close next: per query significance tests, capped recall, Pyserini BM25, and a BM25 plus bge hybrid.

narration.prompt: Explain it to someone outside machine learning.
narration.script: Search engines can find documents in two ways: by matching keywords, or with neural models that try to understand meaning. A well known 2021 study found that neural models trained on web searches often did worse than plain keyword matching when moved to new kinds of documents, like scientific papers. I rebuilt that study myself on my laptop, on two collections of scientific and medical papers. Every published number I checked came back. One score first came out about 18% too low, and I tracked it down to a hidden setting that made one model read only the opening sentences of each paper, with no warning anywhere. Fixing it matched the original exactly. I also found that a newer, smaller model now beats keyword search on both collections.

narration.prompt: How did you know it was truncation and not something else about DPR?
narration.script: I had a positive control first. TAS-B went through the same loader, metrics and search code and matched the paper exactly, so the fault had to be DPR specific. Then I ablated four ways of building the document text at the shipped settings. Title only scored 0.261, title plus full text 0.260. If adding the abstract changes nothing, the abstract isn't being read. The script logs the encoder's max_seq_length at load, and it was 100. Raising it step by step moved the score up steadily to 0.318 at 512, and recall to 0.727, both exactly the published values. A monotone climb that lands on two metrics at once is hard to explain any other way.

narration.prompt: Why exactly does nDCG@10 behave so differently on the two datasets?
narration.script: Because of how many relevant documents each query has. SciFact averages 1.1, so nDCG@10 is basically the position discount of one document: rank 1 scores 1, rank 3 scores 0.5, rank 11 scores nothing. Any damage that pushes it down shows immediately. NFCorpus averages 38.2 graded relevant documents, so the ideal top 10 is full, and if truncation knocks some out, others take their place. The headline barely moves. Recall@100 is less forgiving, and on NFCorpus it did show the bug, 0.190 against 0.208. So I'd check both metrics and at least two datasets with different judgement density.

narration.prompt: Why do you trust your BM25 if it isn't the paper's implementation?
narration.script: I trust it for the conclusion, and I don't claim it's exact. It matches the paper's parameters, k1 0.9 and b 0.4, the Lucene idf, Porter stemming and Lucene's stopwords. It differs in fields and length encoding: one concatenated field instead of two, and exact lengths instead of Lucene's one byte norms. The result is plus 0.012 on SciFact and minus 0.005 on NFCorpus, opposite signs, which looks like implementation noise. The ordering against TAS-B and DPR is unchanged on both datasets, so the paper's conclusion doesn't depend on it. Running Pyserini would close the gap; it needs Java, which I didn't have.

narration.prompt: What does this mean for a production RAG system?
narration.script: Most RAG pipelines chunk by characters or words, then embed with a model that silently truncates at its token limit. If chunks run past the limit, the end of every chunk is invisible to retrieval, and nothing errors. You just see weaker retrieval and blame the model. I'd add three guards. Tokenise every chunk with the embedding model's own tokenizer at index time and fail the build if more than a small share exceed the limit. Log the loaded max_seq_length instead of trusting the model card. And keep a cheap canary like mine: on a labelled sample, full text retrieval should beat title only, and if it doesn't, something is cutting text.

Silent quality loss, no error

narration.prompt: Isn't this just you misconfiguring a model and then fixing your own mistake?
narration.script: Partly, and I say so: the fix is one line. But the 100 was the public port's shipped default, so anyone who loads that model by name gets it. There was no error and no warning, and the output looks like a weak model rather than a broken pipeline. On NFCorpus the headline metric hid it completely, so a single dataset replication would have certified the wrong configuration. What I'd defend is the process: a positive control, a hypothesis list, an ablation that found the tell, and a sweep that matched both metrics to three decimals at the setting the paper says it used.

narration.prompt: Two datasets out of 18 and no significance tests. Why should I trust any conclusion?
narration.script: Trust the narrow conclusion and not more. Two datasets can't stand in for BEIR's 18, and I don't claim they do. For the reproduction itself, significance testing matters less than it sounds: fixed checkpoints and exact search are deterministic, so the right configuration should land on the published number, and the four dense cells do, within 0.001. Where I would want tests is the additions, the hybrid's 0.010 gain over BM25 on SciFact and bge's lead. pytrec_eval already computes per query scores, so a paired bootstrap is a small change, and it's first on my list.

cards.q: Why does this question matter? One plain sentence, then the technical version.
cards.easy: Teams pick between keyword search and neural search all the time, and BEIR is the result most people cite to say neural search trained on one domain does not transfer; knowing whether that still holds, and where it breaks, changes real design choices.
cards.deep: BEIR's claim is about zero shot generalisation: dense retrievers trained on MS MARCO look strong in domain but, evaluated on 18 heterogeneous datasets with no target domain training, often fall behind BM25. Practitioners use that result to justify BM25 baselines, hybrid search, or domain adaptation. Rebuilding it tests three things a reader cannot get from the paper: whether the numbers survive a different machine and implementation, which defaults the paper relied on implicitly, and whether the conclusion still holds for newer models. Here the answer was yes for the paper's models, no for a 2023 embedder (bge-small beats BM25 on both datasets), and the disagreement in one cell exposed a truncation default that applies to almost any retrieval system whose chunks exceed an embedding model's configured limit.
evidence: portfolio: The paper holds for the models the paper tested. It does not survive a 2023 embedder: bge-small-en-v1.5, at 33M parameters, beats BM25 on both datasets.

cards.q: How is the BEIR benchmark designed?
cards.easy: BEIR collects 18 retrieval datasets from very different domains, takes search models that were trained on one large web search dataset, and tests them on all 18 without any further training. Every dataset is converted to the same simple file format and scored with the same metric.
cards.deep: Design choices: (1) zero shot evaluation: most models are trained on MS MARCO (passage retrieval, 8.8M passages) and evaluated out of domain with no target training; MS MARCO results are reported but excluded from the zero shot comparison. (2) Heterogeneity: 18 English datasets across 9 tasks (fact checking, biomedical IR, QA, argument retrieval, duplicate questions, citation prediction, and others), deliberately varied in domain, query length, document length and judgement density. (3) One format: corpus.jsonl, queries.jsonl and qrels/<split>.tsv. (4) One metric: nDCG@10, because rank unaware metrics (precision, recall) and binary rank aware metrics (MRR, MAP) do not handle graded relevance; computed with the Python bindings of trec_eval. (5) Model families: lexical (BM25 via Anserini), sparse (DeepCT, SPARTA, docT5query), dense (DPR, ANCE, TAS-B, GenQ), late interaction (ColBERT), reranking (BM25 plus a cross encoder). (6) Neural models see only the first 512 word pieces of each document. The paper's finding: BM25 remains a strong zero shot baseline; reranking and late interaction score best on average at high compute cost.

cards.q: Describe SciFact and NFCorpus: sizes, queries, relevance judgements, and quirks.
cards.easy: SciFact pairs scientific claims with the research abstracts that support or refute them; each claim has about one correct abstract. NFCorpus pairs short health questions from a nutrition website with medical papers, and each question has dozens of relevant papers at different strengths.
cards.deep: SciFact (BEIR test split): 5,183 abstracts, 300 queries (expert written claims), binary relevance, 1.1 relevant documents per query, average query 12.37 words, document 213.63 words. NFCorpus: 3,633 documents (mostly PubMed), 323 test queries harvested from NutritionFacts.org, 3 level graded relevance derived automatically from the site's links (direct citation, citation via another article, shared topic tag), 38.2 relevant documents per query, average query only 3.30 words against documents of 232.26 words. Consequences: SciFact's nDCG@10 hinges on where one document lands, so it is sensitive to any ranking damage; NFCorpus queries are short lay phrases against technical text, a vocabulary mismatch that hurts lexical matching, and its many relevant documents per query make capped and plain Recall@100 diverge. Loading: beirdata.py downloads the official zips from public.ukp.informatik.tu-darmstadt.de, reads corpus.jsonl (title, text), queries.jsonl and qrels/test.tsv (skipping the header, keeping the integer grade), and keeps only queries the split judges, which is what BEIR does.

cards.q: Why these two datasets, and what did choosing two buy you?
cards.easy: They are the two smallest scientific text datasets in BEIR, so the whole experiment fits on a laptop in minutes. Having two very different ones turned out to matter: the truncation bug showed up on one and hid on the other.
cards.deep: Practical reason: corpora of 5,183 and 3,633 documents can be encoded by three dense models on a laptop GPU in minutes, and exact brute force search over them is trivial, so no ANN index or cluster is needed. cards.q: Write the BM25 scoring function and explain k1 and b.
cards.easy: BM25 scores a document by adding up, for each query word it contains, how rare the word is across the collection times a count term that grows with repetitions but levels off, adjusted so long documents do not win just by being long. k1 controls how fast repeats stop helping; b controls how strongly length is penalised.
cards.deep: $\mathrm{score}(q,d)=\sum_{t\in q}\mathrm{idf}(t)\cdot\frac{tf_{t,d}\,(k_1+1)}{tf_{t,d}+k_1\left(1-b+b\,\frac{|d|}{\mathrm{avgdl}}\right)}$, with Lucene's $\mathrm{idf}(t)=\ln\!\left(1+\frac{N-df_t+0.5}{df_t+0.5}\right)$, which stays positive even for terms in more than half the documents. The tf term saturates at $(k_1+1)$ as $tf\to\infty$; small $k_1$ (0.9 here) means the second and third occurrence add little. $b\in[0,1]$ interpolates between no length normalisation ($b=0$) and full normalisation by $|d|/\mathrm{avgdl}$ ($b=1$); 0.4 is mild. BEIR uses Anserini's defaults $k_1=0.9$, $b=0.4$; Lucene's own BM25Similarity defaults are 1.2 and 0.75, which is a common source of silent mismatch between toolkits. The $(k_1+1)$ factor is a per term constant and does not change rankings, which is why some implementations drop it. Assumptions: term independence (a bag of words), and relevance signalled by exact term overlap after normalisation, which is what fails when queries and documents use different vocabularies.

cards.q: How is BM25 implemented in this repo, and how fast is it?
cards.easy: A short Python file lowercases and splits text into words, drops 33 common words, reduces words to their stems, builds an index from each word to the documents containing it, and scores a query by adding up contributions from those lists. Indexing and searching all of SciFact took half a second.
cards.deep: src/bm25.py: analyze() lowercases, tokenises with the regex [a-z0-9]+, removes the 33 word Lucene EnglishAnalyzer stopword set, and Porter stems with PyStemmer. index() builds postings token -> (doc ids, term frequencies) as numpy arrays with a precomputed idf, plus exact document lengths and avgdl. search() keeps a dense score vector of size N, adds idf * tf(k1+1)/(tf + k1(1-b+b|d|/avgdl)) for each query token's postings (vectorised numpy indexing), then np.argpartition for the top 100 and a stable sort, and drops zero score documents. Title and body are concatenated with a space into one field. Cost: indexing is linear in corpus tokens; a query costs the sum of its terms' posting lengths plus O(N) for the partition. cards.q: How does dense retrieval with a dual encoder work, and how does it differ from a cross encoder?
cards.easy: A dual encoder turns the query and every document into a vector separately, ahead of time for the documents, and ranks documents by how closely their vectors match the query's. A cross encoder reads the query and document together, which is more accurate but has to run once per pair, so it is used to rerank a short list.
cards.deep: Dual (two tower) encoder: $s(q,d)=E_Q(q)^\top E_D(d)$ (dot) or $\cos(E_Q(q),E_D(d))$. Document vectors are computed once and indexed; a query costs one encoder pass plus a nearest neighbour search, exact ($O(Nd)$ per query) or approximate (FAISS, HNSW). Pooling turns token states into one vector: CLS pooling (TAS-B, DPR) takes the first token's state; mean pooling averages tokens. Symmetric models share one encoder (TAS-B, bge); asymmetric ones use separate question and passage encoders (DPR). A cross encoder scores $f([q;d])$ with full attention between query and document tokens, which captures exact interactions but cannot precompute anything, so it reranks the top k of a first stage; BEIR's BM25 plus cross encoder row (0.688 SciFact, 0.350 NFCorpus) is the strongest in its table for these datasets. Failure modes of dual encoders: one vector must summarise a whole document (truncated at max_seq_length), domain shift from the training distribution, and rare terms or exact identifiers that lexical matching handles better.

cards.q: What is DPR, how was it trained, and what does that imply for how you encode documents?
cards.easy: DPR is a 2020 question answering retriever with one network for questions and one for passages, trained to put a question's vector close to the passage containing its answer. It was trained on short Wikipedia passages written as title, a separator token, then text, so documents should be fed to it the same way.
cards.deep: Karpukhin et al. 2020: two independent BERT base uncased encoders, CLS representation, $d=768$, similarity = dot product $E_Q(q)^\top E_P(p)$. Loss: negative log likelihood of the positive passage against negatives, $-\log\frac{e^{s(q,p^+)}}{e^{s(q,p^+)}+\sum_j e^{s(q,p_j^-)}}$. Negatives: in batch (the other questions' positives, so a batch of B gives B squared pairs) plus one BM25 hard negative per question. Passages: Wikipedia split into disjoint 100 word blocks, each prepended with the article title and a [SEP] token. BEIR uses the Multi checkpoint, trained on NQ, TriviaQA, WebQuestions and CuratedTREC, the weakest dense model in its table (0.318 SciFact, 0.189 NFCorpus). Implications Tanay used: encode documents as 'title [SEP] text' (doc_join in DenseSpec), score with dot product, and use separate query and context models (doc_model set). The 100 word training passages are a plausible reason the sentence-transformers port of the context encoder ships with a 100 token limit; that link is an inference, not documented in the port.

cards.q: What is TAS-B, and why does it generalise better than DPR?
cards.easy: TAS-B is a small, fast dense retriever trained on Microsoft's web search dataset with two teacher models guiding it and a clever way of building training batches. In BEIR it was the best dense model, close to BM25 on these two datasets.
cards.deep: Hofstatter et al. 2021: a 6 layer DistilBERT dual encoder, CLS pooling, dot product, 512 token limit (sentence-transformers/msmarco-distilbert-base-tas-b). Training on MS MARCO combines (1) topic aware sampling: queries are clustered once and each batch is drawn from one cluster, so in batch negatives are on topic and therefore harder; (2) balanced margin sampling of passage pairs; (3) dual teacher distillation: a pairwise Margin-MSE loss from a cross encoder teacher plus an in batch negative loss from a ColBERT teacher. Trainable on one consumer GPU in under 48 hours. BEIR reports it beats DPR on 17 of 18 datasets and speculates the distillation loss is why; it also notes TAS-B prefers short documents. In this replication TAS-B reproduced exactly on both datasets (0.643 and 0.319), which made it the control that cleared the pipeline when DPR missed.

cards.q: Why score TAS-B and DPR with dot product but bge with cosine? What goes wrong if you mix them up?
cards.easy: Each model was trained with one way of comparing vectors, and it only ranks well when used the same way. Using the wrong one can make a good model look bad, which is an easy way to fake a negative result about neural search.
cards.deep: Dot product $q^\top d=\|q\|\|d\|\cos\theta$ lets the document vector's norm carry signal; a model trained with dot product (TAS-B, DPR) can encode something like confidence or document salience in $\|d\|$. Normalising those vectors (cosine) throws that away and changes rankings. A cosine trained model like bge produces vectors whose norms are not meaningful, so raw dot product would let arbitrary norm differences reorder results. The rule in dense.py is per checkpoint: DenseSpec.similarity is 'dot' for TAS-B and DPR and 'cosine' for bge, and cosine is implemented by normalize_embeddings=True followed by the same matrix product. The README calls getting this wrong the easiest way to manufacture a fake negative result about dense retrieval. The same care applies to query instructions (bge) and to asymmetric encoders (DPR's separate question and context models).

cards.q: Define nDCG@10 precisely, including gain and discount, and work an example.
cards.easy: nDCG@10 looks at the top 10 results, gives credit for each relevant one, gives less credit the further down it appears, and divides by the best score possible for that query so every query lands between 0 and 1. The final number is the average over queries.
cards.deep: $\mathrm{DCG@10}=\sum_{i=1}^{10}\frac{g_i}{\log_2(i+1)}$, where $g_i$ is the qrels grade of the document at rank $i$ (0 if unjudged). trec_eval uses the grade itself as the gain (linear gain, no $2^{g}-1$) and the discount $\log_2(\text{rank}+1)$. $\mathrm{IDCG@10}$ is the DCG of the ideal ordering of all judged relevant documents, and $\mathrm{nDCG@10}=\mathrm{DCG@10}/\mathrm{IDCG@10}$, averaged over queries. SciFact example, one relevant document: rank 1 gives 1.0, rank 2 gives $1/\log_2 3=0.631$, rank 3 gives 0.5, rank 10 gives 0.289, rank 11 or worse gives 0. So SciFact nDCG@10 is close to the mean discount of one document's position, which is why it reacts sharply to ranking damage. NFCorpus, about 38 graded relevant documents: IDCG fills all 10 slots, and losing one relevant document from the top 10 moves the score by a fraction of that. Why BEIR chose it: it handles graded and binary relevance with one metric, unlike MRR and MAP.

cards.q: Define Recall@100, plain and capped, and why the difference matters on NFCorpus.
cards.easy: Recall@100 asks what share of the relevant documents appear in the top 100 results. The capped version stops penalising a query that has more than 100 relevant documents, since no system could return them all in 100 slots.
cards.deep: Plain: $R@100=\frac{1}{|Q|}\sum_i\frac{|\mathrm{top}_{100}(A_i)\cap A_i^\star|}{|A_i^\star|}$. Capped (BEIR Appendix G): denominator $\min(100,|A_i^\star|)$, so a query with 500 relevant documents can still reach 1.0 instead of being stuck at 0.2. They agree whenever a query has at most 100 relevant documents, which is every SciFact query (1.1 per query on average) but not every NFCorpus query. Capped is always at least plain, so on NFCorpus a plain number below the published capped one is expected even for an identical ranking. Here BM25 NFCorpus recall is 0.246 against a published 0.25, while TAS-B and DPR match 0.280 and 0.208 exactly, so the capping effect is small. Recall@100 matters as a first stage metric: it bounds what a reranker over the top 100 could ever achieve.

cards.q: What is Reciprocal Rank Fusion, why k = 60, and work an example.
cards.easy: RRF merges several ranked lists by giving each document points based only on its position in each list, more for higher positions, and adding the points up. Documents that several systems agree on rise to the top. The constant 60 keeps any single list's top pick from dominating.
cards.deep: $\mathrm{RRF}(d)=\sum_{r\in R}\frac{1}{k+r(d)}$ with $k=60$ (Cormack, Clarke and Buettcher, SIGIR 2009). Example: a document ranked 1 by BM25 and 5 by TAS-B scores $1/61+1/65=0.0318$; one ranked 3 by both scores $2/63=0.0317$; one ranked 1 by BM25 and absent from TAS-B's top 100 scores $1/61=0.0164$. Agreement beats a single strong vote. With $k=60$ the gap between rank 1 and rank 10 is only $1/61$ against $1/70$, so the fusion is flat near the top and lower ranks still count; Cormack et al. fixed 60 in a pilot, found it near optimal, and found the choice not critical (pilot MAP 0.2072 at $k=0$, 0.2145 at 60). Why rank based: BM25 scores (unbounded, query dependent) and dense dot products live on incomparable scales, and RRF needs no normalisation, weights or training data. Failure modes: it ignores score margins, so a confident system and an unsure one count equally, and if one input is much weaker it can drag the fusion down.

cards.q: How is the hybrid implemented?
cards.easy: Take the top 100 from BM25 and the top 100 from TAS-B for each query, give every document points for its rank in each list it appears in, add them up, sort, and keep the best 100.
cards.deep: src/evaluate.py rrf(runs, top_k, k=60): for each query ID in the union of runs, iterate each run's ranked list with rank starting at 1, add 1/(k + rank) to the document's total, sort by descending total with document ID as the tiebreak (deterministic output), and truncate to top_k = 100. A document missing from one list simply gets no contribution from it, which is equivalent to an infinite rank. run.py picks the dense partner as the first available of tas-b, bge-small, dpr, so the reported hybrid is BM25 + TAS-B, the paper's two strongest single models on these datasets. No scores are combined, so no normalisation is needed. Cost is negligible: two lists of 100 per query. It is evaluated with the same pytrec_eval call as every other system.

Step 2, enumerate DPR specific hypotheses: the join between title and text, asymmetric encoders, and how much of the document the context encoder sees. Step 3, ablate: src/ablate_dpr.py encodes SciFact four ways (space join, [SEP] join, text only, title only) and logs the encoders' max_seq_length at load. At the shipped limit of 100 tokens: space 0.260, [SEP] 0.276, text only 0.171, title only 0.261. Title only matching title plus text means the body contributed nothing measurable, the signature of truncation. Step 4, confirm: sweep max_seq_length (100, 256, 350, 512) and watch both metrics climb to the published values at 512. Total sweep cost about 20 minutes on the laptop.

cards.q: What does max_seq_length actually do, and why was the truncation silent?
cards.easy: Every embedding model reads at most a fixed number of word pieces; anything longer is cut off, and the library does it without complaint. The DPR document model was set to 100 pieces, while a typical SciFact abstract is a couple of hundred words, so most of each abstract was never read.
cards.deep: In sentence-transformers, inputs longer than model.max_seq_length are truncated to the first max_seq_length tokens at tokenisation; there is no warning because truncation is the intended behaviour for long inputs. The limit is per checkpoint configuration and can be lowered or raised up to the transformer's positional limit (512 for BERT base). Tokens are WordPiece units, so 100 tokens is fewer than 100 words; the docs put 512 tokens at roughly 300 to 400 English words. SciFact abstracts average 213.63 words in BEIR's statistics, so a 100 token cap keeps roughly the title and the first sentences. The port of DPR's context encoder shipped with 100; TAS-B and bge ship with 512, which is why they were unaffected. Why it is dangerous: the output is a perfectly normal ranked list with plausible scores, and the metric drop looks like a weak model rather than a broken pipeline.

Space join: 0.260 at 100, 0.287 at 256, 0.302 at 350, 0.310 at 512. Decomposition of the original 0.058 gap (space at 100 to [SEP] at 512): length alone is worth +0.050 with a space join or +0.042 with [SEP]; the join is worth +0.016 at 100 tokens and +0.008 at 512. So truncation is the dominant cause and the separator is a smaller, real second cause, consistent with DPR's training format of title [SEP] passage. dense.py's note attributes the whole 0.058 to truncation, which is slightly generous; the precise split is above. Matching on two metrics at once, nDCG@10 and Recall@100 to three decimals, is much stronger evidence of the right configuration than matching one.
cards.say: At 100 tokens with the separator, DPR scored 0.276. At 512 it scored 0.318, exactly the paper, and recall matched too, 0.727. Most of the gap was length; the separator token was worth about 0.008 to 0.016 on top.

cards.q: Why does 512 reproduce the paper exactly, and why might the port ship with 100?
cards.easy: The BEIR authors fed every neural model the first 512 word pieces of each document, so setting DPR to 512 recreates their setup. The 100 likely comes from how DPR was originally trained, on 100 word passages, though that is an inference.
cards.deep: BEIR's experimental setup states that, because of transformer length limits, it uses only the first 512 word pieces of every document for all neural architectures. So the published 0.318 was computed at 512, and the shipped 100 silently changed the experimental condition. DPR itself was trained on Wikipedia split into 100 word blocks, each prefixed with the title and [SEP]; a port that sets max_seq_length = 100 is consistent with that training regime, which works for 100 word Wikipedia passages and fails for 200 word scientific abstracts. Tanay labels the origin of the 100 as plausible, not documented. The general lesson: a model's shipped inference configuration encodes assumptions from its training data, and those assumptions do not travel with the model to a new corpus.

cards.q: Why was the bug invisible on NFCorpus? Was it entirely invisible?
cards.easy: NFCorpus questions each have dozens of relevant papers, so damaging the ranking a bit still leaves plenty of relevant papers in the top 10, and the headline score barely moved. The recall number did show the damage, in hindsight.

cards.q: Where else does this failure mode show up, and how would you guard against it in a production RAG system?
cards.easy: Any search system that splits documents into chunks and embeds them can hit the same problem: if a chunk is longer than the model's limit, the end of the chunk is never seen, with no error. The guard is to measure chunk lengths in the model's own tokens and alert when they exceed the limit.
cards.deep: Where it bites: RAG pipelines that chunk by characters or words (say 1,000 characters or 300 words) and embed with a model whose max_seq_length is 256 or 512 tokens; long titles plus body; non English text, which tokenises into more pieces; code and tables. The retrieval still works, so the symptom is a quality loss that looks like a weak model. Guards: (1) tokenise every chunk with the embedding model's tokenizer at index time and log the share over the limit; fail the build above a threshold; (2) log the loaded max_seq_length per model, as ablate_dpr.py does, instead of trusting a model card; (3) chunk by tokens with the model's limit minus a margin; (4) a cheap canary like the one that caught this: compare title only against full text retrieval on a labelled sample, and expect full text to win; (5) evaluate on at least two datasets with different judgement density and track two metrics. Tanay's portfolio states the same failure is waiting in most retrieval systems whose chunks exceed the configured limit.
evidence: portfolio: The same failure mode is waiting in any retrieval system whose chunks are longer than an embedding model’s configured limit, which is most of them.

cards.q: Isn't the truncation bug just you misconfiguring the model? Why call it a finding?

cards.q: What are the limitations, and what breaks at 10x and 100x scale?
cards.easy: The limits are two small datasets, single runs without significance tests, a substitute BM25, and plain rather than capped recall. At bigger scale the laptop runs out: encoding millions of documents needs GPUs, the score matrix needs an approximate index, and the Python keyword index needs a real search engine.
cards.deep: Limitations: 2 of 18 datasets; BM25 not Anserini (one field, exact lengths); plain Recall@100; no per query statistics; additions (bge, RRF) are single configurations. At 10x (around 50,000 documents, still small): exact search stays fine, encoding grows linearly (DPR at 512 tokens would take roughly 35 to 40 minutes on this laptop by linear extrapolation from 219.5 s), and BM25's dict of numpy postings still fits memory. At 100x and beyond (BEIR's large corpora reach millions of documents; MS MARCO has 8.8M passages): 8.8M x 768 float32 vectors is about 27 GB, beyond a laptop, so vectors need fp16 or product quantisation and an ANN index (FAISS IVF or HNSW), which turns exact recall into approximate recall that must itself be measured; encoding needs GPUs and batching by length; BM25 needs Lucene or another compiled engine with on disk postings; and evaluation needs per query outputs stored for significance testing. Production retrieval would add query latency budgets, index refresh, and the chunk length guard from the truncation lesson.

cards.q: Define zero shot retrieval, in domain versus out of domain, and MS MARCO.
cards.easy: Zero shot retrieval means using a search model on a new kind of collection without training it on that collection. In domain means testing on data like the training data; out of domain means testing on something different. MS MARCO is a large Microsoft dataset of real Bing questions and web passages that most neural search models are trained on.
cards.deep: Zero shot (in BEIR's sense): the model receives no training examples from the target dataset; its parameters come from other data, typically MS MARCO passage ranking (about 8.8M passages, 532,761 training pairs, binary judgements, about one relevant passage per query). In domain: evaluation on MS MARCO dev, which BEIR reports but excludes from the zero shot comparison. Out of domain: the 18 BEIR datasets, which differ in domain (biomedical, finance, scientific claims), query style (questions, claims, short titles), document length and judgement density. The gap between in domain and out of domain scores is the generalisation gap BEIR measures. DPR is a special case here: it was trained on open domain QA datasets, not MS MARCO.

cards.q: Define word pieces, max_seq_length, CLS pooling and embedding normalisation.
cards.easy: Word pieces are the sub word units a model reads; long or rare words split into several. max_seq_length is how many of them the model will read. CLS pooling uses the model's summary token as the document's vector. Normalising scales every vector to length 1 so dot product becomes cosine similarity.
cards.deep: WordPiece (BERT family) splits text into a 30k unit vocabulary; 'microstructure' may become several pieces, so token counts exceed word counts, especially for technical text. max_seq_length: the sentence-transformers truncation limit, at most the model's positional limit (512 for BERT and DistilBERT); inputs beyond it are cut without warning. CLS pooling: the final hidden state of the [CLS] token, which models like DPR and TAS-B were trained to make a sequence summary; mean pooling averages token states instead and is used by many other embedders. Normalisation: $\hat v=v/\|v\|_2$, after which $\hat q^\top\hat d=\cos(q,d)$; dense.py sets normalize_embeddings only for cosine models.

cards.q: Define an inverted index, Porter stemming and stopwords.
cards.easy: An inverted index maps each word to the list of documents containing it, so a query only touches documents that share a word with it. Stemming cuts words to a common root, so 'treatments' and 'treated' can match. Stopwords are very common words like 'the' that are dropped because they carry little meaning.
cards.deep: Inverted index: term -> postings list of (doc id, term frequency), plus document lengths; query cost is proportional to the posting lengths of the query terms, not the corpus size. bm25.py stores postings as numpy arrays for vectorised scoring. Porter stemmer (1980): rule based suffix stripping in steps ('caresses' to 'caress', 'ponies' to 'poni', 'relational' to 'relate'); it raises recall and occasionally conflates unrelated words. Here it comes from PyStemmer's Snowball implementation of Porter, matching Anserini's Porter setting. Stopwords: the 33 word Lucene EnglishAnalyzer list (a, an, and, are, as, at, be, but, by, for, if, in, into, is, it, no, not, of, on, or, such, that, the, their, then, there, these, they, this, to, was, will, with). Note 'no' and 'not' are dropped, which matters for claims like SciFact's, where negation flips meaning; BM25 cannot see it either way.

cards.q: Define qrels, a run, and judged queries, in BEIR's format.
cards.easy: Qrels are the answer key: for each query, which documents are relevant and how strongly. A run is a system's output: for each query, a ranked list of documents with scores. A judged query is one that has at least one entry in the answer key.
cards.deep: BEIR layout: corpus.jsonl rows {_id, title, text}; queries.jsonl rows {_id, text}; qrels/test.tsv with a header and columns query-id, corpus-id, score (an integer grade; binary 1 for SciFact, graded for NFCorpus). pytrec_eval expects qrels as {qid: {doc_id: int}} and a run as {qid: {doc_id: float}}. Only queries present in the test qrels are scored, so queries.jsonl entries without judgements (training queries, for example) are dropped by beirdata.load. Unjudged documents in a run count as non relevant, a known bias against systems that retrieve good documents the original judges never saw, which matters more for new models than old ones.
